analysis.one_liner: Requires the U.S. to ratify a treaty banning all nuclear weapons and redirect that spending to human needs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 8 Democratic cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would commit the United States to sign and ratify the United Nations Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which calls for every country to eliminate its nuclear weapons under international control. It would then shift the money currently spent on nuclear weapons programs into retraining weapons-industry workers and funding things like health care, housing, education, and clean energy. It would only take effect once the President certified that all nuclear-armed countries had started dismantling their arsenals. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, the main beneficiaries would be ordinary people through a peace dividend: resources now spent on nuclear weapons would be redirected to health care, housing, education, agriculture, environmental restoration, and carbon-free energy development. [S3] Workers in the nuclear weapons industry would get retraining and a transition into a 'peace economy.' [S3] Whether any of this ever happens depends on every other nuclear-armed country joining in, since the bill's spending provision only takes effect after the President certifies that all countries with nuclear weapons have begun eliminating them. [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Directs the U.S. government to sign and ratify the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons or a similar agreement eliminating all nuclear weapons in every country under strict international control. [S2] [S3]

Redirects nuclear weapons program resources toward converting weapons plants and retraining employees for an 'ecologically beneficial peace economy,' including strict control of fissile material and radioactive waste. [S3]

Routes redirected funds to human and infrastructure needs, including sustainable carbon-free and nuclear-free energy, health care, housing, education, agriculture, and environmental restoration with long-term radioactive waste monitoring. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The nuclear weapons industry — the companies, laboratories, and plants that design, build, and maintain the arsenal — would lose the revenue streams this bill redirects. [S3] The defense establishment broadly would lose a core mission, and the change would come with real transition costs for the communities built around weapons work, which the bill tries to soften with retraining provisions. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill's core spending provision only takes effect after the President certifies that all nuclear-armed countries — including Russia and China — have begun eliminating their arsenals, so U.S. unilateral disarmament is not the mechanism; but critics would argue that committing to a treaty the other eight or nine nuclear powers have not joined could weaken deterrence. [S3]

Nuclear weapons policy is set through treaties ratified by the Senate and through defense authorization law; a bill directing the executive branch to ratify a sweeping disarmament treaty cannot by itself accomplish that, so the measure is largely a statement of principle rather than an enforceable plan. [S2] [S5]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it ever took effect, the bill's appeal is a large peace dividend — tens of billions of dollars a year moved from weapons to human needs — and it thoughtfully pairs abolition with worker retraining and cleanup of radioactive waste. The honest objection is that it rests on every other nuclear power disarming in step, which no negotiated framework has yet achieved, and a single bill cannot bind future presidents or the Senate. It was introduced as a statement of principle, and it got one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Foreign Affairs and Armed Services Committees and to a Strategic Forces subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021. [S5]

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on April 30, 2019, with 8 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support. [S1] [S4]
It was referred to the Foreign Affairs Committee and, for the provisions in its jurisdiction, the Armed Services Committee. [S5]
A week later it was referred to the Armed Services Subcommittee on Strategic Forces — the panel that handles nuclear weapons — where it stayed. [S5]
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2021. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nuclear weapons industry and the defense programs it supplies are better off: nothing changed, and the money the bill would have redirected kept flowing to weapons programs. [S3] [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters — the sponsor and 8 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote so party positions were never formally tested. [S4] [S5]

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons industry and weapons complex contractors
industries.note: The bill redirects the funding that flows to weapons plants, programs, and laboratories into health care, housing, and clean energy, ending their core revenue source. Their interest in the bill's fate ran against the peace dividend ordinary taxpayers would have received. [S3]

industries.industry: Clean energy, health care, and infrastructure sectors
industries.note: Redirected weapons spending would fund carbon-free energy deployment, health care, housing, and environmental restoration — the same services the public would consume. [S3]
